Diaphyseal Forearm Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Fractures of forearm and wrist are the most common types of pediatric skeletal trauma,
accounting for approximately 30% to 40% of all pediatric fractures.
Most commonly the result of a fall on an outstretched hand
Most can be managed via closed reduction and cast immobilization.
Careful attention must be paid to the radiocapitellar joint and the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ)
during assessment so Monteggia or Galeazzi fractures are not missed, especially if radiographs
demonstrate a seemingly isolated radial shaft or ulnar shaft fracture.
Epidemiology
Forearm fractures account for as many as 18% of all pediatric fractures1 (Resource 1).
Increased childhood obesity has led to increased failure of nonsurgical management2
(Resource 2).
Forearm fractures are associated with elbow fractures in 10% to 15% of patients.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most forearm shaft fractures result from a fall onto an outstretched hand.
Angular and rotational deformities often are present.
Associated Injuries

Plastic deformation is traumatic bowing of the forearm as a result of trauma. This is
more common in children younger than 10 years. Patients often have minimal clinical
deformity or pain but loss of forearm rotation. On imaging studies, no fracture is
identifiable; however, the bones no longer maintain the normal contours. On lateral
radiographs, bowing of any degree in the radius and ulna is considered abnormal. On AP
radiographs, decreased interosseous space or excessive ulnar bowing may indicate
plastic deformation. Contralateral radiographs aid in identifying injury by allowing for
comparison of the injury radiograph with that of the patient’s normal radius and ulna.
Greenstick fractures are incomplete fractures and are common in children. They should
be described as apex volar or apex dorsal to guide reduction. They have a predictable
rotational deformity also used to aid in reduction. The fracture of the radius and ulna
usually is at slightly different levels, indicating the rotational component. Complete
fractures are categorized similar to those in adults based on fracture location, pattern,
angulation, and displacement (Resource 3).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Obtain a patient complete history, including time of injury, mechanism, of injury location of
pain, neurologic status of the arm, previous treatments/attempted reductions, and any
medications received.
Physical Examination
Always perform a physical examination on the uninjured side first so the patient will know
what you are doing, which will help alleviate anxiety and aid in compliance with the
examination.
Assess the skin. Open wounds often are punctate or poke hole and are commonly missed. Any
bleeding near the fracture site should increase concern.
Assess for tenderness to palpation, including the joint above and below the fracture to not
miss other injuries. This is best done before assessing the injured and painful fracture.

Neurovascular Examination
Palpate for radial artery and capillary refill
Complete neurologic examination
Median nerve
Motor: abduct the thumb
Sensory: volar tip of thumb/index finger
Anterior interosseous nerve: flex at the thumb interphalangeal joint and the index finger
distal interphalangeal joint
Ulnar nerve
Motor: abduct index finger against gravity (without wrist flexion)
Sensory: volar tip of the little finger
Radial nerve
Motor: extend the thumb at the interphalangeal joint and the fingers at the
metacarpophalangeal joint with the wrist straight
Sensory: dorsal thumb and first web space
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Obtain AP and lateral radiographs of the injured forearm.
The radial styloid should be 180° opposite from the bicipital tuberosity, indicating rotational
alignment.
The ulnar styloid should be approximately 180° opposite the coronoid; however, this may be
difficult to assess radiographically in young children with an unossified ulnar styloid.
Mismatched cortex and bone width at the fracture site may indicate malrotation.

Radiography
Ensure orthogonal views of the elbow and wrist are obtained in the forearm
radiographic series so a Monteggia or Galeazzi fracture is not missed. If concern for a
subtle fracture (like bowing) exists, then radiographs of the contralateral side should be
obtained for comparison. If an isolated radius fracture is present, the wrist must be
assessed for DRUJ disruption (Galeazzi fracture) with the use of dedicated orthogonal

present, the elbow must be assessed for radial head subluxation/dislocation (Monteggia
fracture) with the use of dedicated orthogonal elbow radiographs and a focused physical
examination.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Most pediatric forearm fractures can be managed nonsurgically via cast immobilization.
Cast immobilization for 6 weeks is typical in younger children; however, cast immobilization for
as long as 10 to 12 weeks may be necessary in older children.
Indications
Shaft angulation greater than 20° in children younger than 8 years or greater than 10° in
children older than 10 years.1
Rotational deformity greater than 30° to 45°
Malrotation does not remodel.
Bayonet apposition with 100% displacement is well tolerated and remodels.

Indications
Recommendations for reduction are based on fracture location and patient age. Less
angulation is acceptable the farther the fracture is from the physis because the
likelihood for remodeling is decreased. Less angulation is acceptable in older patients
because of decreased time for remodeling. Adequate remodeling is not expected in
patients within 1 to 2 years of skeletal maturity. Angular malunion of the proximal radius
and rotational malunion results in loss of forearm rotation. Loss of rotation of 30° to 45°
rarely affects function.
Techniques/Procedures

Ensure adequate sedation in the emergency department or the operating room if attempting
reduction.
In general, Greenstick fractures are rotational injuries. Attempting to correct angulation
alone will be incomplete for both injuries.
Apex volar fractures (supination injuries) are reduced via forearm pronation.
Apex dorsal injuries (pronation injuries) are reduced via forearm supination.
Rule of thumb: rotate the thumb to the apex of the angular deformity
Complete fractures require reduction of the angular and rotational component
Increase angular deformity while applying traction, and then perform reduction maneuver
to correct angulation and rotation.
As much as 1 cm of bayonet apposition may be tolerated if angular alignment is acceptable.
Immobilize in an above-elbow cast or a plaster sugar-tong splint
Fractures typically are managed via 6 to 8 weeks of cast immobilization.
Fracture alignment should be assessed on AP and lateral radiographs for at least the first 2
weeks.
If loss of reduction occurs in the first 2 weeks, the cast should be wedged or completely
replaced in clinic to improve alignment.

Techniques/Procedures
A three-point mold is used to maintain fracture reduction. The cast must be narrower in
the volar-dorsal plane than in the radial-ulnar plane by a ratio of 0.7 or less on
radiographs. This is called the cast index (Figures 2 and 3; Table 1). Casts with a cast
index higher than 0.7 have an increased risk for loss of fracture reduction. The elbow is
placed at 90° with the use of straight posterior and ulnar cast borders to hold the cast in
position. Increasing evidence supports cast immobilization of proximal third fractures in
extension to aid in reduction and maintenance of alignment.

Shaft angulation greater than 20° in children younger than 8 years or greater than 10° in
children older than 10 years1
Rotational deformity greater than 30° to 45°

Relative indications include older age, higher energy injuries with greater soft-tissue injury,

Substantially displaced fractures in adolescents are at high risk for re-displacement and are a

Indications
The need for surgical versus emergency department irrigation and débridement in
patients with a poke hole and Gustilo grade I open fracture is controversial. Small series
have shown that such injuries may be managed via irrigation and débridement in the
emergency department followed by reduction and antibiotic agents. This is not indicated
if the patient fell in a dirty environment. Contaminated wounds or Gustilo grade II or
grade III open fractures require surgical irrigation and débridement, often followed by
surgical fixation because these higher energy injuries are unstable and lack the soft-
tissue envelope and periosteum necessary to maintain reduction in a cast.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Obtain adequate preoperative radiographs.
Have intramedullary implants of the correct size and plates available.
Can use titanium or stainless steel flexible nails or smooth Steinman pins
Have C-arm available.

Patient Positioning
Supine with a hand table
Surgical Approaches
Radius: volar forearm approach for plate placement
Ulna: ulnar approach
Mini-open approach for reduction; usually is adequate for nails
Surgical Fracture Fixation
Most fractures can be managed via intramedullary fixation.
Internal fixation with the use of intramedullary devices or plates is associated with a high rate
of success in children (Figure 4).
Flexible nails
Dorsal or radial starting point in the distal radial metaphysis proximal to the physis
Ulnar starting point at the tip of the olecranon or the radial aspect of the ulnar shaft near the
olecranon through the anconeus
Use a mini-open approach and reduce the fracture site if unable to pass the nail after three
attempts2
High rate of compartment syndrome with multiple unsuccessful passes of the nail
Fixation of one bone often is adequate to stabilize an unstable forearm, particularly in children
younger than 10 years2,3 (Figure 5 ).

Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Limit the number of attempted passes of the intramedullary device to reduce risk of
compartment syndrome.
Care should be exercised with the entry point of the radial intramedullary device to decrease
the risk of injury to the extensor pollicis longus (dorsal entry) or the superficial branch of the
radial nerve (radial entry).
Complications
Malunion
Malunion is unusual if serial radiographs are obtained during the first 3 weeks after fracture.
Loss of pronation/supination is common but usually mild.
Fracture
Refracture occurs in 5% to 10% of children who undergo management of a forearm fracture.

Fracture
The highest risk for refracture is within the first 6 months postinjury. Refracture most
commonly occurs at the middle third followed by the proximal third of the forearm. Risk
of refracture increases with more than 15° of residual deformity (Resource 4).
Other Complications
Compartment syndrome
Risk factors for compartment syndrome after fixation of both-bone forearm fractures include
high-energy injuries and multiple attempts at reduction and rod passage.
Risk of injury to the extensor pollicis longus tendon with dorsal entry point for the radial nail
2.6% incidence
Risk of injury to the superficial branch of the radial nerve with radial entry point for the radial
nail
2.9% incidence

Pseudo-Volkmann contracture because of undetected tethering of the flexor digitorum
profundus muscle belly in the fracture site after reduction. This can be avoided by passively
extending the fingers after reduction to assess for possible tethering.4
Infection after open fracture
Overall infection rate for grade I open pediatric fractures is 1.9% to 4%.5
For grade I forearm fractures, many studies support local irrigation and débridement with
the use of betadine and intravenous antibiotic agents in the emergency department followed
by an outpatient course of oral antibiotic agents, which results in negligible infection rates.
Delayed union
Higher rate in children 10 years and older who have an open fracture
Outcomes
Excellent rate of healing with intramedullary fixation and plate fixation

Outcomes
Plate fixation typically is indicated for comminuted fracture patterns, in older
adolescents with closed physes, and for the management of nonunion.
Distal Forearm Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Fractures of the distal forearm and wrist are common.
Isolated distal third radius fractures may have a concomitant disruption of the DRUJ (Galeazzi
fracture-dislocation).
Angulation and displacement in the sagittal plane have substantial remodeling potential;
angulation and displacement in the coronal plane have less remodeling potential.
20° to 30° of angulation in the sagittal plane in patients younger than 10 years is acceptable.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:55 PM
AAOS | Diaphyseal Forearm Fractures, Distal Forearm Fractures, and Monteggia Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001057
15/44


Overview
Fractures of the distal forearm and wrist are some of the most common injuries in
children. These include metaphyseal and physeal injuries and account for as many as
30% of fractures in children. Because of the proximity to the physis, these injuries have a
remarkable ability for remodeling. Subsequently, based on a patient’s age, a certain
degree of angulation can be accepted. In general, 30° of angulation in the sagittal plane
is acceptable in a patient younger than 10 years ; however, remodeling of even greater
angular deformity has been observed in very young patients. Less remodeling potential
exists the coronal plane. The older the child and the farther the fracture from the physis,
the less remodeling potential is available.
A rare but often missed distal forearm fracture is a Galeazzi fracture-dislocation. This
represents a disruption of the DRUJ in an isolated distal third radius fracture, usually
with dorsal dislocation of the ulna. Galeazzi fracture-dislocations must be suspected in
patients with an isolated distal third fracture to ensure appropriate management. In
skeletally immature patients, the Galeazzi equivalent may be associated with a Salter
Harris fracture of the distal ulna. A risk of ulnar physeal arrest and the need for open
reduction exists because the metaphysis may become buttonholed by the extensor carpi
ulnaris tendon or the periosteum.
Epidemiology
Mean patient age is 10.9 years.
Incidence is 1.5 times greater in males then females
The physis is involved in one-third of pediatric distal forearm fractures.
Galeazzi fracture-dislocations are rare, accounting for less than 3% of fractures in children
Peak incidence between 9 to 13 years


The mean age of patients with a distal forearm and wrist fracture is 10.9 years. The
incidence is 1.5 times higher in males than in females, with the top five activities
associated with these fractures including bicycling, football, playground activities,
basketball, and soccer. Injuries in children from birth to 12 months are most commonly
associated with beds or bed frames. Injuries in children aged 13 to 36 months are most
commonly associated with stairs. Children aged 11 to 17 years had fractures most
commonly associated with playing football. An increased incidence of pediatric distal
radius fractures is associated with decreased bone density, increased body mass index,
participation in higher energy activities, and participation in higher energy activity at a
younger age.
Galeazzi fracture-dislocations account for less than 3% of fractures in children, with a
peak incidence occurring between the ages of 9 and 13 years.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The most common mechanism of injury is a fall onto an outstretched hand.
Injury Classification
Metaphyseal fractures
Buckle/torus fractures—The cortex is intact on all radiographs; however, an indentation may
be observed on the compression side (Figure 6). Radiographs must be carefully evaluated to
not to miss a subtle fracture line extending to the opposite cortex.
Complete fractures--A break in the cortex is observed on at least one radiographic view
(Figure 7).

Figure 8 Illustrations show the Salter-Harris classification of physeal fractures. Type I is
characterized by a physeal separation. Type II is characterized by a fracture that traverses the
physis and exits through the metaphysis. Type III is characterized by a fracture that traverses the
physis before exiting through the epiphysis. Type IV is characterized by a fracture that passes
through the epiphysis, physis, and metaphysis. Type V is characterized by a crush injury to the
physis. (Reproduced from Kay RM, Matthys GA: Pediatric ankle fractures: Evaluation and
treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2001;9[4]:268-278.)
Galeazzi fracture—A distal radius fracture with disruption of the DRUJ and subluxation or
dislocation of the ulna (usually dorsally; Figure 9).

Injury Classification
Metaphyseal fractures can be categorized as buckle fractures or complete fractures.
Buckle fractures are inherently stable with the cortex intact on all radiographic views. An
indentation but not a complete break of the cortex may be observed. Complete fractures

these two fracture patterns is important so a complete fracture is not managed via

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Obtain a complete patient history, including time of injury, mechanism of injury, location of
pain, neurologic status of the arm, previous treatments/attempted reductions, and any
medications received

Always perform a physical examination on the uninjured side first so the patient will know
what you are doing, which will help alleviate anxiety and aid in compliance with the
examination.
Assess the skin. Open wounds often are punctate or poke hole and are commonly missed if
not evaluated by an orthopaedic surgeon. Any bleeding near the fracture site should increase
concern.
Assess for tenderness to palpation, including the joint above and below the fracture to not
miss other injuries.
Neurovascular Examination
Palpate for radial artery and capillary refill
Complete neurologic examination
Median nerve

Overview
Disruption of the radiocapitellar joint, with fracture or deformity of the ulna.
Monteggia fractures are infamous for being missed. The provider must maintain a high index
of suspicion for a Monteggia fracture in any child with radial head subluxation or dislocation or
an isolated ulnar shaft fracture. Isolated radial head dislocations almost never occur in
children. Presumed isolated injuries almost universally result from plastic deformation of the
ulna with concomitant radial head dislocation, which is the most common pattern of a missed
Monteggia fracture-dislocation.

Ulnar nerve injuries associated with Bado type II injuries

Injury Classification
The Bado classification describes the direction of radial head dislocation (Figure 11). This
usually follows the apex of the ulna fracture or deformity. Bado type I injuries are an
anterior radial head dislocation with apex anterior ulnar angulation. Bado type I injures
are the most common (70% to 75%) and usually result from a fall onto an outstretched
hand with the forearm in pronation. Bado type II injures are a posterior radial head
dislocation with apex posterior angulation of the ulna, causing tension on the ulnar
nerve. Bado type II injuries are rare and account for only 3% to 6% of injuries. Bado type
II injuries result from an axial load on a partially flexed elbow or from direct trauma to
the proximal supinated forearm. Bado type III injuries are a lateral radial head
dislocation with a varus angulated proximal ulna fracture (apex lateral). Bado type III
injuries are the second most common fracture pattern (15% to 20%). Bado type III
injuries result from a fall on an outstretched hand with the forearm in pronation and
varus stress. The laterally dislocated radial head puts the posterior interosseous nerve at
risk for injury. Bado type IV injuries are an anterior radial head dislocation with a
proximal third transverse fracture of the radius and ulna. Bado type IV injuries result
from a fall onto an outstretched hand with the forearm in pronation and usually result
from a higher energy mechanism of injury.

Fracture Fixation
Usually, restoration of ulnar length results in reduction of the radial head. Therefore, the
ulna is addressed first. If the fracture is transverse or short oblique, then an
intramedullary nail with the entry site at the tip of the olecranon or the radial aspect of
the ulnar shaft near the olecranon usually is adequate to hold reduction. Ensure
correction of any residual bowing or deformity of the ulna, which may result in inability
to maintain radial head reduction. After the ulna is reduced, the radial head usually
reduces. If the radial head does not reduce after reduction of the ulna, then the
radiocapitellar joint should be opened to ensure no interposing soft tissue is blocking
the reduction. Very rarely does the annular ligament need to be reconstructed. If ulnar
length cannot be maintained with the use of an intramedullary nail, then plate fixation is
required. Radiocapitellar reduction must be confirmed in multiple planes and
throughout elbow range of motion (flexion/extension and pronation/supination). A
transcapitellar pin is not recommended as an aid to maintain reduction because of
problems such as implant failure, postoperative stiffness, and radial head osteonecrosis
(Figure 14).

Chronic fractures
Because long-standing, chronic Monteggia fractures are associated with pain, instability,
limited range of motion, and tardy nerve palsies in adults,2 surgical reconstruction usually is
recommended. Results are better if this is accomplished within 3 years postinjury or in
children younger than 12 years.

Contralateral radiographs of the uninjured arm

Preoperative Planning
If a chronic Monteggia fracture is fully healed and the ulna has remodeled, contralateral
radiographs of the uninjured arm may help reveal ulnar deformity for surgical planning.
The ulna usually heals in a shortened and extended position. MRI may aid in assessing
the shape of radial head and the capitellum in patients with a longer standing chronic
injury to determine whether congruent reduction can be attained. The radial head
becomes convex or rounded and the capitellum becomes hypoplastic in patients with a
long-standing dislocation.2
Fracture Fixation
Ulna often requires osteotomy with plate fixation to correct shortening and angular deformity.
Obtaining ulnar length is as important as overcorrecting the angular deformity.
Open radial head reduction usually is required to débride fibrous tissue and the scarred
annular ligament that precludes reduction.
Annular ligament repair rarely is required if the radial head will not maintain reduction after
correction of ulnar length and deformity.
